subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This government was elected. If they want the opposition to provide the solution, that is another thing. But it is a most amazing and fatuous way of dealing with the problem. This government was elected to govern, and they turn around and ask us what we would do. What a way to act! This motion indicates that nothing is being done to deal with the problem of inflation. It sets out, in its provisions with regard to the resource industries, to rend this country apart and strike at the heart of confederation. Madam Speaker, I commend this motion to all members of the House, those who want to think about it, those who go beyond blind adherence and cupidity in so far as the policies of this government are concerned.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a great privilege for me to have the opportunity to take part in this debate on the budget. I believe this is one of the most crucial and difficult budgets a Canadian finance minister has ever had to present. It comes at a time when the international financial and economic situations are in a state of turmoil and near chaos, when there is an increasing sense of frustration and despair, and when there has been a significant slowdown in economic activity while inflation continues to rage and the balance of payments deficits of oil importing countries soar to potentially disastrous levels.
While it is true that Canada has not been as directly affected as many countries in terms of oil imports and crop failures-which are the major causes of the present international predicament-still, due to our position as one of the world's great trading nations, we are extremely vulnerable to the unpredictable winds of international economic developments. With this background of uncertain and adverse developments from abroad, the minister's normally difficult task of providing economic and fiscal leadership and direction for Canada has increased immeasurably. However, it is my belief that he has succeeded admirably.
Madam Speaker, my training has qualified me in several spheres. However, the few economics courses which I took in university, and my not always successful attempts at managing the household budget, are not sufficient to enable me to discuss Monday evening's budget in the detail which I would like. However, there are many on both sides of this House who do possess the qualifications to do so, and I look forward to their comments with interest and no small degree of envy. For my part, I would like to discuss the budget in terms of its impact on the constituents I represent.
Toronto-Lakeshore, the constituency I have the honour to represent, is situated in the borough of Etobicoke, one of the six boroughs which comprise metropolitan Toronto. The trouble with representing a Toronto riding is that everyone lumps you in with the 20 or so other Toronto ridings. However, while many concerns and interests are common to all metro ridings, the degree and intensity of these concerns differ from constituency to constituency, and while the people may not readily identify with a federal electoral district as such, they do identify with communities and neighborhoods within that district. It is in the setting of these communities and neighborhoods
November 21, 1974

that interests and problems are articulated and priorities established.
In Toronto-Lakeshore there are six distinct communities: Mimico, New Toronto, Long Branch, Alderwood, Queensway and Sunny Lea. Undoubtedly, the predominant concern of the people of these communities, as it is with most Canadians, is inflation measured in terms of soaring food prices, lack of moderately priced housing, record high mortgage rates and the day to day battle between the individual's pay cheque and rising costs. However, because of the economic, social and demographic composition of the communities, their priorities, although sometimes similar, often differ from those of other metro ridings.
The constituency I represent has a high percentage of senior citizens and, as such, measures to protect this group from inflation are continually being pushed. I was particularly pleased to see two such measures in the throne speech, namely, the elimination of the earnings test on retirement pensions for persons aged 65 to 70, and the payment of allowances to spouses aged 60 to 65 of old age security recipients.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not enough.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may not be enough, but at least it is a start in the right direction. The budget contains a number of measures which should go a long way in lessening the impact of inflation on our senior citizens. The $1,000 exemption for interest and dividends, although available to all taxpayers, will have an especially beneficial effect on the elderly, who very often have much greater dependency than others on this form of income. The $1,000 deduction for pension income will come as a welcome tax relief to the elderly.
The same is true of the provision which will permit the transfer of the age exemption from one spouse who does not require it to the other who does, when completing the income tax return. I would like to see more of this kind of realistic and practical government flexibility in other programs. A final point before leaving this subject. I hope the government will act during this session to provide increased funding for senior citizens housing. There is a great need for more of this type of housing in my constituency, and I am sure this is true of many other constituencies.
However, I must say I was pleased with the emphasis the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) placed on housing in his budget. The proposal to produce 200,000 houses or more per year is commendable. The reduction of the sales tax on building and construction materials to 5 per cent, and the removal of the sales tax on construction equipment and on materials used in municipal water distribution systems should reduce the cost to the home buyer. The registered home ownership savings plan and the $500 grants to those purchasing new, moderately priced housing units will enable more Canadians to purchase a home. These measures and others contained in the budget should provide much needed stimulus for residential construction.
Another aspect of the housing situation which has attracted a considerable amount of interest in Toronto-Lakeshore is development designed to rejuvenate existing homes and neighborhoods; for example, the Laburnam
The Budget-Mr. Robinson
project. I commend the Department of Urban Affairs for the increasing emphasis it is placing on this kind of project and ask them to encourage more such projects in the future. I would hope that Laburnam would be followed through and completed.
Madam Speaker, the overwhelming proportion of my constituents are middle-income earners many of whom are unionized. There has been a growing demand among union members that some form of cost of living allowance- COLA-provision be written into their labour agreements. There are certain serious weaknesses with the COLA provision, such as the consumer price index which is the basis of measurement and tends to underestimate the effects of inflation on lower income groups and overestimates its impact on higher income groups. Nevertheless, it remains perhaps the only acceptable mechanism to protect workers committed to long-term contracts.
While I am on this general subject I would like to say a few words about the growing number of strikes and lockouts, particularly in the public sector. I feel the public's patience and understanding in this regard is nearly exhausted. In terms of their number, disrupting effects and cost, strikes have reached an intolerable level. The point has been reached where management, labour and government must seek other alternatives. I am hopeful that before this parliament is over, progress in this direction will be made.
I have mentioned that a high proportion of my constituents are middle-income earners in the $8,000 to $15,000 a year range. During the past year or so I believe there has been growing resentment among this group; young couples beginning a family, the trained, experienced workers buying a home, and university graudates starting their careers feel that government has forgotten them or, worse, is taking them for granted. These people find themselves caught in the middle at budget time, with tax relief going to the lower income groups in order to assist them with inflation and to business enterprises in order that they may sustain or expand economic activity and employment opportunities. They feel their hard-earned tax dollars are spent on programs aimed at other groups and other interests, and too often they find serious abuses and inefficiencies in these programs.
Although I do not agree entirely with these sentiments, the fact is that this is how a growing number perceive the situation. This middle-income group has traditionally been the strongest supporter of social programs and legislation. However, I fear a backlash has been developing against certain such programs. Without the support of Canada's middle-income earners, new, needed social legislative measures will be in jeopardy, if not doomed. The government must act to wipe out abuses and inefficiencies in existing programs. In the same light, it must show or ask companies to show that tax concessions and other assistance to large businesses are not just increasing profits but, rather, are creating more employment and/or providing reduced prices to the consumer.
We must again provide some form of incentive for middle-income earners, incentive which many of them believe is now absent. All too frequently I come across university

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Robinson
graduates who are on unemployment insurance or welfare. They find the opportunities to employ their talents are too few, the rewards too small and the alternatives both attractive and available; that is, welfare and unemployment insurance. I believe the budget which the minister presented Monday offers more to the middle-income earner than has been offered by any other budget in a good many years. A great many of my constituents will be able to look at a number of measures which are contained in this budget and say, "That is good for me." The most obvious of these measures are the personal income tax cuts. While the greatest benefits will be received by lower income earners, and rightly so, these tax cuts, both this year and in 1975 will assist most Canadians.
I have already mentioned other measures which will directly assist many middle-income earners, such as the housing initiatives aimed at reducing the cost and increasing the accessibility of home ownership, the interest and dividend deductions and other proposals such as the Canada Savings Bonds provisions which are designed to protect an individual's savings. In addition, there is the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on adult clothing and footwear, implemented last July by order in council, along with sales tax reductions on a number of items ranging from buses to bicycles. I congratulate the minister for the removing such tax. I know that metropolitan Toronto will benefit from this measure: we need many buses and a great deal of subway equipment and I am happy to note that such equipment will not be subject to tax.
Although the Minister of Finance did not specifically mention in his budget speech the needs of the Canadian forces, I should like to do so at this time. It is my understanding that to perform the tasks outlined in the 1972 report, the Canadian forces will require a minimum strength of 82,000 personnel, together with the replacement of obsolete and obsolescent equipment, as well as the provision of new, sophisticated equipment required to keep our forces up to date. I hope the minister will also find funds to provide the expertise, ships, planes and ground forces to more adequately guarantee our sovereignty from sea to sea and in fact from our shores to the 12-mile limit and even out to the 200-mile limit, because we must project our fishing rights and the environment.
I began, Mr. Speaker, by giving a brief description of the world's severe economic situation which was the setting for the budget. The Minister of Finance said that the world is "in a fragile and precarious state, suffering from severe inflation and the gathering forces of recession." I should like to conclude by saying that the need for international co-operation has never been greater, if we are to avoid international catastrophe. This need for co-operation and joint action was reflected during the past year by such gatherings as the Law of the Sea Conference in the summer, the recent World Food Conference at home and other international economic meetings.
Unfortunately, the potential of these gatherings has been undermined by petty national and regional jealousies and interests. Just last week we had a demonstration of this with the United States placing quotas on beef and pork. History has shown that attempts to provide this kind of unfair protection for national producers during periods of economic uncertainty have snowballed, resulting in

economic and social disaster for the international community.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance for his budget presentation last Monday night. It provides needed leadership and determination in the fiscal field, yet contains the flexibility needed to cope with unforeseen international developments. The measures incorporated in it will, I believe, have a beneficial impact in the fight against inflation while at the same time guarding against recession. Finally, I see the budget as an optimistic appraisal of Canada's potential and, at the same time, a realistic assessment of the dangers we must face.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) took it upon himself to show the government team in its true light. Within a few hours, the minister served-us a speech, that is the budget speech which, while professing to be a government program, constitutes paradoxically a condemnation of the government by the government.
Throughout his speech, the minister managed to expose the hoax the people had already started to suspect. He recognized having misled Parliament through his erroneous forecasts, which he naturally attributes to others, the international context, the weather, poor crops throughout the world, monetary difficulties, market fluctuations, the price of gold and God knows what else!
He admitted having deceived the people who do remember that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once condemned the removal of the 11 per cent tax on building materials. He particularly deceived the population by suggesting that he would lead a fierce battle against inflation, while today, dropping the gloves and worrying about a possible recession rather than about the present inflation, he leaves the battle before the first round has even been called.
Mr. Speaker, ever since 1968 until now, the Liberal government never had the intention nor the desire to control inflation. Never mind that, we, under the leadership of the leader of the opposition, to whom I wish to pay a tribute for the stirring speech he made in the House yesterday, will not give up.
One need be neither astute nor very suspicious to see this budget as the first step in a carefully planned and orchestrated game, a game that the Liberals have been playing for some time with our country and our federation. This budget, if we look at its highlights and provisions carefully, treats inflation as a trifle, something to acknowledge but not really worth seriously worrying about. The various provisions of the budget move in every direction so imperceivably that it is impossible to glean exactly the direction in which the government is going or the direction the country should follow.
This document comes from those wonderful people who offered Canada leadership, that strange, elusive quality that only the Liberals can offer and, as we were told by their hucksters, only they can deliver. This budget has done for statesmanlike leadership and economic leader-
November 21, 1974

ship what the Boston strangler did for door to door canvassing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, let us leave this staring gap in the budget provisions and look closely at the one thing about which there is no doubt in this budget no doubt in the mind of the Minister of Finance and no doubt in the mind of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The big red machine, in all its grandeur and arrogance, is picking a fight. Those gunslingers, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, with the itchy trigger fingers have saddled up and are eager to do battle with the people of Alberta. In any event, the big red machine seems prepared to fire the first shot and keep its guns loaded.
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, they figure that Alberta is Alberta and only Tories come from Alberta, so why not take them on. The real people, the Liberals' heartland of support-the golden triangle and central Canada-will be proud of the way the big red machine takes on the oilmen of Alberta: it might even push the machine a few points up in the polls.
Let us consider who the brave Minister of Finance is really aiming at in his budget. Alberta and her rights to the development of secondary industry and a renewable and consistent economic base happens to be one target. But there are others. What about Newfoundland and her hopes for royalties and development, thanks to her resources; or Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick? They, too, are directly implicated: they are directly in the line of the big red machine's sputtering cannon. Indeed, what this finance minister who rides high in the saddle has really done is cast a pall of smoke over the growing hopes of maritimers for the type of mineral and resource wealth that recent encouraging finds have given them every reason to build their hopes and aspirations on for the future. Of course, when one notes how much patronage the big red machine would lose if the maritimes enjoyed an economy that DREE would not have to support, one can understand the big red machine's desire to scuttle any hopes there.
The people of Quebec, how well they are served by their gunslinging representatives in the federal cabinet! The Quebec caucus of the big red machine may think that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are taking aim at Alberta, but closer examination reveals that those Quebec members who think they are looking out over the gunsights at Alberta are really looking into a mirror.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How they serve confederation! How they stand "solide", as they used to say, as their leader takes away their province's mineral and resource rights, along with those of other provinces! The Minister of Finance always boasts that he seeks example budgets from many Canadians of all walks of life. That is, indeed, an admirable practice for such a straight-shooter. But I have to wonder-indeed, I have to ask-whether the section on resource taxation read by the minister in the House might not have been written by Rene Levesque. As a former resource minister, Mr. Levesque knows full well how much Quebec's prosperity and economic growth depend on
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
its natural resources, and that a threat to those resources would aid in so many ways the separatist cause.
No province, no territory, no group of Canadians who seek or enjoy improved services through their provincial government can escape the effects of the budget's implications. It is, as I said, an old game, a game steeped in victory for the red machine, a game bathed in cynicism and deceit. The Liberals have always liked what confrontation does for them politically. They have always liked painting things black and white, choosing sides and watching the opinion polls come their way. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) did it in 1973 during the energy crisis that never was, and indeed the red machine's figures at the polls jumped high enough for them to coast home in July of 1974.
The Prime Minister, when minister of justice, built his reputation on confrontation with his own province. In more devious fashion they did the same thing in 1970, overreacting and spreading panic by their own extremism. But oh how their popularity soared and they coasted through on that. I would like to have more belief in this government, more belief of this Minister of Finance; but I say there is no basis in fact for any faith whatever.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a basis in fact and a basis in history to believe that this government will seek in every way to manipulate this battle, to exaggerate its proportions and to extenuate its circumstances so as to reap maximum partisan gain. Our hope, Mr. Speaker, lies in the ability of Premier Lougheed and the other provincial premiers to work out meaningful options based more on public interest than the self-serving options of this minister and his government.
Once again I say that leadership is not being exercised by the federal government-only brinksmanship of the worst order. Leadership in the form of statesmanship will have to come from other sources and other major levels of government in Canada. My leader exposed yesterday the duplicity of this government, duplicity which covers everything from personal conduct-I need not give any examples-to insincerity of commitment and purpose.
This budget is another example of that manipulative ability, common to Liberals, to divide the nation while campaigning as great unifiers once the divisions they have begun are established. They have sought to divide Francophone from Anglophone when it has suited their purpose. Now they have returned to their old target-confederation itself. As the government seeks to divide Canada into easterners and westerners, producers and consumers, exporters and importers, as they seek to label their enemies and patronize their friends, as they seek to wreak dissension and disunity, I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that your compatriots and mine will remember that, above all, we are Canadians-Canadians who have worked out our problems before, patched up our differences and risen above the chameleon qualities of the demagogue and the political huckster.
They will recall how long we have striven to achieve the unity of purpose and sanity of approach which have pro-

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
tected and nurtured our nation's growth and development. Let us remain resolved that these little men who sit opposite shall not tear us asunder.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a verse in a very well known song by Gilbert Becaud which says: The train we take always takes us somewhere. Well, the train of the supporting measures which are found in the budget speech of November 18 is taking Confederation straight into bankruptcy.
I want to consider for a while the interference of the federal government into the area of natural resources, for this is indeed a case of real interference.
After having pondered over the possibility of meddling with exchange markets, carried out, through its URBEX projects, a general offensive in the area of urban planning, tried to lay its hands on the income which may flow from the development of off-shore mineral deposits, the government becomes excessively centralist in a number of chapters of the communications file, assuming increasingly more jurisdiction in a clearly cultural area, interfering at the level of territorial development through its community programs and what have you. This federal administration has finally decided to deliberately and off-handedly tackle the provincial governments through its taxation of resources.
By brutally asserting that royalties, taxes and other payments to provincial governments will no longer be deductible from taxable income at the federal level, the present federal government itself is violating the national energy agreement reached last March or, at the very least, is jeopardizing the survival of national consensus in the name of equity between east and west.
Of course, this way it is first of all reneging on the deal with the producing provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. But, at the same time, it is calling down upon itself the collective anger of the premiers of this country. The government, by this violation of the spirit and the letter of British North America Act section 109, is opening the door to a major constitutionnal conflict which will have a decisive effect. Reactions are already piling up and I shall spare the House that subject. In fact, they are coming from all corners of the country.
It is equally clear that Ottawa is looking for a confrontation and will get it.
Assuredly the present federal government, besides putting aside the limits that it imposed upon itself when formulating the long promised and awaited-for policy which is self-evident if we consider Bill C-32 and the new budget, wishes and is looking for a showdown. To be sure, if they had wanted one they would not have done otherwise.
With the government refusing to allow royalties paid to provinces as deductions for federal income tax purposes, the Prime Minister of the country has proved his inadequacy in building Canada's more and more complex future. It might well be that he is not interested in it anymore.

Here we are in Canada, Mr. Speaker, with a Prime Minister presumably elected in 1968 to tighten the bonds of national unity and he is speaking pocketbooks when he is talking about a policy which could lead Confederation to the brink of the precipice.
It is under the same Prime Minister who boasted of taming the Parti Quebecois, of "having no good done" to young impatient Quebecers and who at first was elected because of that, that Quebec has seen its independentist movement rise like a meteor. He has no more managed to tame the P.Q. than he has managed or wants to manage to tame inflation. It is under this same Prime Minister that western alienation is gaining steam.
Had the present paradoxical, cynical, Machiavellian, Prime Minister of this country chosen to prove the nonviability of Confederation, he would not have proceeded otherwise.
The Minister of Finance in his unilateral approach in the field of resource taxation missed a fine opportunity to both promote exports and loosen up federal-provincial relationships.
The Trojan horse that has become the equalization program-there is talk of $253 million more for Quebec, but that is not sure-must not put to sleep either provincial governments or responsible authorities. One Trojan horse trick in history is enough.
Before concluding, because I will not be repeating here points that would be relevant to this debate that I had ample opportunity to express on November 4 last, I like to think that the Quebec government in particular will not be prepared to sell its rights. Let it realize that one day it could be its turn. Let it not wait to react firmly, officially and publicly. Let it not wait until the federal government glances at the power and mining resources in Quebec. The claims, and even more so, the legitimate aspirations for any "sovereignty", for obtaining increased powers, must all resist the federal millions.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps for the first time in the history of this country, provincial governments must understand and use the weapon of disinterested, total and open solidarity on an acceptable compromise in face of a central government which seems to be stricken with political panic and whose recent reelection can already be viewed as the greatest disservice in modern times Canadians did themselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing this budget at a time when the world faces more serious problems than it has faced at least since World War II. In the underdeveloped parts of this world- Asia, Africa and South America-hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of people face death by starvation. In the industrialized part of the world-North America, western Europe and Japan-we see recession on its way or presently existing. Italy and Great Britain are faced with financial crises the like of which they have not seen for the last 200 years. Japan, that post-World War II miracle, is faced with unemployment and a sharp increase in costs with which they do not know how to deal. Our neighbour to the
November 21, 1974

south, the United States, a country to which we sell' most of our exports and from which we import more than any other country in the world, is now in a recession.
Let me put on the record a couple of paragraphs from last Sunday's New York Times outlining the situation in the United States. Industrial production-output of factories, utilities and mines-dropped six-tenths of 1 per cent in October, but this figure does not reflect recent large cutbacks in automobile production. During the July-Sep-tember period, the gross national product slipped 2.1 per cent, the third consecutive quarterly decline. During October the dollar total of the country's payroll increased less than in September, a strong sign of recession, says the Times. Automobile sales were off more than 38 per cent in the first ten days of November, a more severe decline than had been expected. Unemployment, 6 per cent in September, continued to rise. And so on.
Despite these facts, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) brings down a budget essentially the same as the one that he presented in May, six months ago. The minister is engaging in parlour games while forces are massing which can shake this country to its roots. Yet the minister picks this very time to enter into a constitutional debate with the provinces, the consequences of which no one can foresee, with perhaps a battle in the courts that will take years to resolve. Instead of getting together with the provinces in order to work out an agreement to share revenue collected by the federal government as a result of the sharp increase in oil prices, the Minister of Finance makes a unilateral decision which in my view is constitutionally not permissible.
Instead of the government dealing with the real economic problems facing the country, this parliament, the press, radio and television as well as the public are to become engaged in the battle between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance with all the provinces. I do not intend to spend much time on this question since members from all parties will be discussing it. I simply say I find it strange that the Minister of Finance is proposing to adopt a policy that will permit Imperial Oil to pay royalties to Canadian Pacific Railway if it drills wells on CPR land, and will permit Shell to pay royalties to American owners of land or to Indonesian owners of land if Shell drills well on the soil of those two countries, yet will not permit those companies to deduct royalties paid as a business expense if they drill wells on land belonging to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. This seems a strange way for the Government of Canada to do business.
In his budget the Minister of Finance is assuming that Canada can avoid the recession that is plaguing other countries. In the little pamphlet issued by the minister entitled "Budget... in Brief", we read the following at pages 4 and 5:
With the benefit of measures in this budget, and with no unforeseen deterioration of the economic environment abroad or unforeseen shocks at home, the Canadian economy is expected to grow at a rate of about 4 per cent in 1975.
That is a completely unrealistic estimate. The OECD has estimated that Canadian growth in 1975 will not be 4 per cent but will be in the neighbourhood of 1 per cent. As a matter of fact, in a report that appeared in the Montreal
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
Gazette a day or two ago, based on statistics issued by Statistics Canada we are told the following:
The government yesterday issued sombre figures on the economy suggesting there was little or no growth in the year's third quarter, and the economy may even have gone into reverse.
With economists forecasting a still poorer performance in the final quarter of 1974, the Canadian economy could face two quarters of negative growth-which would technically qualify as a recession-this year.
What is happening in fact, Mr. Speaker? A couple of days ago Chrysler of Canada announced that 1,700 Chrysler workers in Canada will face lay-offs as a result of the six weeks' cutback in production by the Chrysler Corporation of the United States. If auto sales in the United States do not pick up-as I have already indicated, they have dropped by over 30 per cent-these lay-offs are likely to be extended. At the time when this is happening in Ontario, the number of workers laid off in the forestry industry in British Columbia rose to over 15,000 last week, an increase from 14,719 unemployed at the beginning of the month. The Council of Forest Industries, in releasing these figures, said that the unemployment rate in the industry had reached 17 per cent of the total work force.
This is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, because housing starts in Japan, the United States and Canada have fallen disastrously. The Minister of Finance proposes to do very little about this. What plans does he have to deal with this growing cancer of unemployment and recession? As far as we can tell from his confident, ebullient budget, he has none. Five months have already been lost since his May budget, and I suggest that six months from now we will be presented with another budget which will attempt to deal with the recession into which we are heading.
I suggest that the Minister of Finance should have come before the House this week and said that his department, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the department that deals with housing, are calling on the provincial governments to prepare, now, the detailed plans that are required to be put in effect next March and April to deal with the situation if unemployment continues to grow in Canada. I believe unemployment will increase, and most economists say it will if the recession in the United States, Japan, Great Britain and Italy continues to grow worse, and every indication is that it will.
What the minister should be saying is that he is not prepared to encourage the private sector of the economy by tax concessions, of which it has already had too much, to take up the slack, but if necessary he is prepared to implement plans, which should have been prepared by the provincial governments, to pour into the Canadian economy a sum of money, which economists have estimated should be in the neighbourhood of $2 billion, for direct projects to put people to work doing things and creating facilities required in the form of houses, roads, recreational centres and community projects. These are the things we need.
What has the minister done? He has placed emphasis on expansion of the private enterprise system. He proposes to continue giving massive tax concessions to the corporations of this country whose profits have been and continue to be high. Just a few days ago the Toronto Globe and Mail
1542

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
carried a story, the headline on which was "Profit of Industrial Corporations Shows Smaller Year-to-Year Gain". However, if we read the story we see:
After-tax profit of industrial corporations in the third quarter amounted to $2.31 million, up 27.5 per cent from a year earlier, Statistics Canada reports.
The minister called on workers who will be receiving a $50 tax rebate in the coming year to be moderate in their wage demands. What did he do for the corporations whose profits have increased by 27 lA per cent in the third quarter of this year as compared to the third quarter of last year? He gave them more tax concessions. Mineral fuels, which I presume means the oil and gas corporations, had increased profits of 45.9 per cent in the third quarter of 1974 compared to the third quarter of 1973. For the first nine months of 1974 their profits were up by 37.7 per cent. The minister gives them more tax concessions, but tells the provinces he intends to squeeze them when they try to increase their royalties from oil companies. Then if the oil companies cannot pay more money, the minister says the government will squeeze the provinces rather than the oil companies.
What about the individual? The personal tax reduction and exemptions the minister is proposing are regressive. They provide greater benefit for the higher income groups and will only exacerbate the existing standards in respect of income. The combined effect of tax indexing, the reduction in the rate on the first $500 of taxable income from 12 per cent in 1974 to 9 per cent in 1975, and the general tax rate reduction in 1975 mean that for a single taxpayer with an income of $6,000 the tax saving in 1975 will be $183. For a single taxpayer with an income of $30,000 the saving will be $651. Where is the equity in such a proposal?
In the case of a married taxpayer, with two children under 16 years of age, who has an income of $6,000 the saving will be $214 in 1975. For a similar person with an income of $30,000 the saving will be $622. I wish that the Minister of Finance, when he was thinking about his budget, had read a speech made by his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), because in a speech which that minister made to the Empire Club in Toronto he showed how badly we have dealt with the people of this country. He showed how great the disparity in income still is in this country after all these years of Liberal and Conservative, but mostly Liberal, governments.
Let me summarize what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said in his speech to the Empire Club in Toronto. He noted that in 1972 there were one million families with incomes under $5,500 a year in this country. Those people live in what has been classified by the Senate Committee, headed by a Liberal, Senator Croll, by the Economic Council of Canada and by Statistics Canada, as poverty. Those families, which represent 20 per cent of all the families in Canada, received just 6 per cent of total family income that year. At the same time the 20 per cent of families at the upper end of the income scale, with earnings over $15,400 a year, received 39 per cent of all family income.
The one-fifth of the families at the top of the income scale had incomes which were six and one-half times as large on average as the one-fifth of the families at the

bottom of the scale. These are national totals which do not reveal the even more serious income distribution inequities among people in various regions. However, these figures show clear evidence of the problem which must be faced.
How did the Minister of Finance face this problem? He faced it by increasing the disparity between people at the bottom fifth of the income scale in favour of the top 40 per cent. This is what we have come to expect from Liberal governments and from this Liberal Minister of Finance. In the so-called just society-a phrase I think the Prime Minister wishes he had never picked up from his speech writers-this is the kind of tax proposals we get from the Minister of Finance at a time when we face tremendous inflation.
When people in the bottom 40 per cent of the income scale find it increasingly difficult to pay for the bare necessities of life, the minister comes forward with a budget which will give the greatest benefit to the people in the top income brackets and which will give the least benefit to those at the bottom. It is for these reasons I, and members of this party, certainly intend to oppose the budget, vote against it, and will continue to call on the Minister of Finance to face the real problems of this country which are increasing unemployment, increasing inflation, and increasing poverty for most of the people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think every member of this House has a commitment to all the people of this country. I believe we differ only in the method of achieving the desired ends.
Let me state first of all that I have a great deal of respect and admiration for some hon. members on the other side of the House, especially the hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. members for Halifax, Oshawa, Nanaimo, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I think they will go down in our parliamentary history, as I believe the great progress the Government of Canada has made in past years is due in part to their contributions in this House. However, I cannot understand anyone who suggests that the budget presented the other day is not a good, sound document designed to benefit the majority of the people in Canada.
The people of Canada knew this government would present this kind of budget, and that is why they returned this government to power with a majority. But each one of us here, both on the government side and in opposition, has his own ideas about what is best for Canada and what should be done in the future, and it is during this debate that we make our views known.
So that you, Mr. Speaker, will more fully understand the general content of my remarks, let me first state that I represent the district of Gander-Twillingate in Newfoundland. My district has 88 communities on the map. In actual fact it comprises 146 smaller entities; in some cases three and four separate communities exist under one name on the electoral district map. There are only a dozen of these communities that have any form of industry other than
November 21, 1974

the fishery. In the majority of instances there is no real industry.
All of us here in this chamber look upon the budget in the framework of how it applies to the majority of the people we represent. Within this framework I am concerned about the underprivileged, the primary producers, those on fixed incomes, those who in many cases have not a hope in the world of improving their lot under existing circumstances. For even while we can legislate changes in taxation, income and social benefits, there is no real assurance that the benefits are passed on to the people. There exist the business community and provincial governments which sometimes operate in direct opposition to our legislation.
Let me state first of all that I have been concerned that, mainly because of a vicious taxation structure in some provinces over the past several decades, we have had a regressive tax structure in this country. What does a regressive tax structure mean? On a graph it says that those who make the least, pay the most in real income through taxes in one form or another. I, like other members, have wrestled with this problem for some time. I have conjured up visions of negative income tax and guaranteed annual income structures that would correct this grave injustice.
We must remember, Sir, that while we sit in this chamber a vast minority of our people sit at home wondering where their next dollar will come from; in fact many of these homes have large families and they face a never ending struggle for survival. The real crime respecting their situation rests in the fact that many are primary producers.
On the other end of the scale we have seen, over the past decades, the emergence of the newly rich, those who hold, because of their position in society, monopolies of one form or another. They have become rich because of our system. How did they get their money? Was it by the sweat of their brow? Was it by making two blades of grass grow where one grew before? No, as far as actual production is concerned they do not toil, neither do they spin. They sit in their stylish offices and watch the money roll in, Mr. Speaker.
More people want more. The selfishness of one class of our people must be checked by government. To see the starving millions in this world, for me, as a member of this House, to visit homes in my district where parents and children sit around the table with only bread and tea on it, not even any butter, that is a crime. It makes an even greater crime when, 100 feet away, is the ocean where there are tons upon tons of fish, such as herring, mackerel and capelin. But because private enterprise does not see fit, there are no fish processing plants. In some communities where those fish are being caught, we still operate on the feudal system, as is the case in my district. That is, the boats come in from Norway and other parts of the world, including other parts of Canada, load up the raw material, and send it back to us the next year, canned, charging sometimes 100 times more per pound than it cost the processors.
This government, in two budgets, has tried to right some wrongs. It has attempted to cope with the critical situation of world inflation. It has been among the more successful
The Budget-Mr. G. Baker
governments in doing so. In two budgets it has said, "We will try to correct inequality, we will offer greater social benefits, we will decrease taxation for the majority of our people, and we will try to increase production."
Our course is in the right direction. A guaranteed annual income for all Canadians in some form appears possible in the future.
This is a vast country with a multiplicity of problems, and we cannot always achieve justice. The Treasury Board knows that regional rates of pay for federal employees in Gander do not go over big with me, whereas they are a great thing for western Canada. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) is aware of the fact that to place the same stiff rules on unemployment insurance recipients in Alberta, where 30,000 jobs are vacant, and on recipients in Gander-Twillingate, where no jobs are vacant, is simply not fair play.
The Minister of State in charge of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) realizes that when money was paid for loss of time due to ice last year, those fishermen unfortunate enough to be on welfare because of the ice conditions had that federal money deducted from their provincial welfare cheques.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) knows that family allowances given to those on welfare in Newfoundland are deducted from their welfare cheques, and that the new increase in January will mean nothing to those on the welfare rolls because of provincial regulations.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) knew when he proposed income tax cuts on the federal level that our provincial income tax went up four months ago by 11 per cent.
So, while the federal government is doing its best to equalize opportunity in this nation, the provincial governments have a role to play as well. The position that we hold, of trying to equalize opportunity federally, means that certain provinces have to give more to help other provinces, that certain groups in Canadian society must give more to help others less fortunate than themselves, and that we as a nation must, in the name of humanitari-anism, be prepared to offer our food surpluses to those who are dying of starvation, and the problem of who gets what, when and how, must be dealt with in our method of distributing foreign aid.
What then does this budget do for the long run? We should never be accused of treating the symptoms and not the disease. All governments, for too long, have been blaming the mirror for not being a window when they see such inequalities in this country. The Minister of State (Fisheries) is looking at the income stabilization program for fishermen, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare is looking at some form of guaranteed annual income for Canadians.
The government, in this budget speech, has clearly stated its concern to deal with the real problems. The tax cuts on production equipment, the continual use of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to encourage production, the continuing funding of AHOP, the shifting of the tax burden on to the shoulders of those who can afford to pay, all this augurs well for the future.
28543-29%

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. C. Smith
In the case of my district my duty here in the House, in committees and behind the scenes, will be to try to impress on everyone the importance of the government playing a greater role in initiating industry, looking for the potential resource development areas, and then actively doing what private enterprise will not do. The provincial government of Newfoundland and the federal government have? come together in a co-operative effort to create secondary industry without the immediate rip-off of profit going into someone's pocket.
All the rotten eggs of the Egg Marketing Board do not amount to the value of fish that go untouched in the waters of any one of the outport communities in my riding. The relative importance of many things must find new perspectives. The value of an individual, and his stake in this country, should not be determined by how much money he has in the bank, but better by how many children he has-what is the size of his family.
The 100 per cent write-off for exploration expenditures, the 50 per cent national tax rate for resource industries, the sales tax on building and construction materials reduced to 5 per cent, the capital cost allowance on new, multiple unit residential buildings for rent, to be claimed against any source of income, the federal sales tax on construction equipment and on materials used in municipal water distribution systems eliminated, the new registered home ownership savings plan, the $500 grants for new moderately price homes, the federal sales tax on transportation equipment removed, the two year write-off of new machinery for manufacturing and processing, the first $1,000 of private pension income exempt from tax, a 10 per cent surtax on corporate profits, special excise taxes on high energy consuming vehicles, the elimination of the sales tax on clothing and footwear, new tax incentives for small businesses, and tariff reductions on consumer goods-all will benefit the majority of Canadians, and will go far to eliminate the inequality within and between provinces.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak in the budget debate. While the budget may be of some help to certain areas in Canada I feel it is of little or no help to the people of the Churchill constituency which I represent.
The constituency of Churchill covers some 200,000 square miles of central and northern Manitoba. The population is in excess of 85,000 people spread out over 75 communities. The physical make-up of the communities is as varied as you will find in any part of Canada. The one seaport is the port of Churchill located on Hudson Bay. I say this for the benefit of those members who have not yet visited our area.
The federal and provincial governments are in the process of rebuilding that entire community, with improvements in housing and recreational facilities. This revamping of the community, however, has put a burden on the people in that they are now unable to meet the high taxes and rents required for new housing and recreational facilities.

The town of Churchill has undergone drastic change, but the people there claim they had no part in the planning. This is what happens when governments take over and try to improve facilities and communities; the people are pushed aside. They were given no opportunity to participate in decision-making, nor is there any evidence that they will be given this role in the future as Churchill is now classed as a government-owned and government-run town.
The port of Churchill is the only bright spot in the economic future of this community, but the government is not planning fully to develop and utilize this port. At present it is capable of handling some 40,000,000 bushels of grain during the shipping season, which runs from July 20 to October 20. Due to poor planning by the Wheat Board, however, only 22,000,000 bushels of grain were shipped through the port during the past year.
When grain is sold to a specific country by the Wheat Board I believe that the Wheat Board at that time should designate a date on which the grain is to be taken from the port of Churchill. During last year there were sometimes as many as eight boats in the port of Churchill waiting to be loaded, and at other times there was not a boat in sight for eight or ten days. I think the government should ensure that the facility is used to its full capacity.
A sound economic base must be developed so that people can work for a wage on which they can live. During the election campaign I said that people who live in the north should be given a northern allowance to offset the high cost of living there. An allowance of this nature would be an incentive to attract and keep people in the north.
The budget provisions announced on Monday night will be of little or no benefit to the average wage earner in the Churchill constituency. During the election campaign we heard promises to the effect that the eligibility age for old age pension benefits would be lowered. The budget has come and gone, however, and our senior citizens still have to face those difficult years when they must depend on benefits.
There are some 20 Indians reserves in the Churchill riding, ranging in population from 200 to 2,500. Many of these reserves have no sound economic base. Even though the chiefs and councils have been pleading with the government to help the bands develop industry, meaningful training programs and self-government on the reserves, it appears that most of these requests have fallen on deaf ears, or are tied up in the bureaucratic system. The Indian people are fed up with study upon study-they want action. I would suggest that the government should start to listen to and learn from the various Indian organizations that have made formal presentations.
In 1972 the federal government granted the province of Manitoba-namely, Manitoba Hydro-permission to divert the Churchill River and to control the water levels on Lake Winnipeg and the Nelson River. When the licence was issued, little or no thought was given to the project's detrimental effects on the environment and, most important, the flooding and immersion that will be caused to Indian reserve lands along the Churchill diversion, Lake Winnipeg and the Nelson River. Mr. Speaker, the chiefs of those reserves that are and will be affected are now involved in a legal battle with the province of Manitoba. I
November 21, 1974

feel that the federal government was irresponsible in issuing this licence to the province without considering the effects that such changes in water levels would have on reserves and other communities in the north.
The Indian people affected have not taken this lying down but have formed a committee, called the Northern Flood Committee, to deal with the province of Manitoba concerning the flooding of reserve lands and other problems relating to their fishing and trapping rights. The former minister of Indian affairs and northern development granted funds to the committee, but these are now depleted. The committee has submitted a proposal for further funds to fight the flooding of the reservations. The chairman of the flood committee is in Ottawa today, trying to get funds which were originally promised so that he could continue with his job. As I say, these funds were promised during the campaign. They were to be approved last week, but that approval is still pending.
Let me now deal with mining in the constituency of Churchill. Really, mining is the backbone, the economic base of my constituency. We must always remember that mines are not discovered and developed overnight. The abortive budget of May 6 would have put the small prospector or small mining developer out of business. The budget of November 18 has not changed this situation. Large mining companies in my riding are now as vulnerable as the small prospector or developer.
The high cost of living, together with actions of provincial and federal governments, has squeezed mining companies to the point where they feel they are not getting a reasonable return on invested dollars, and will be forced to cut back. Cities and towns have been built around mines. Many communities are one-industry towns and depend completely on the mining industry. In excess of
35,000	people in northern Manitoba and in the riding of Churchill live in mining towns. These people, I feel, live in such communities because they like living there and because they enjoy a feeling of security.
After the May 6 budget many people living in mining communities became uneasy. They felt insecure and were uncertain about the future. This uncertainty caused many people this past summer to leave mining communities and seek employment in other fields. The result has been a shortage of miners in my riding. The budget of November 18 has further aggravated the sense of insecurity of people working in the mining field.
Governments say they want a fair share of the national pie. Considering the high cost of living, we must ask what is a fair share of the pie? Let me put some figures on record to show what I mean. Both federal and provincial governments in Canada received substantial net benefits from mining development, especially from development in the constituency of Churchill.
The federal government, during a 12-year period, received accumulated revenues of $407 million and spent only $7.8 million, receiving a net benefit of $339 million. Is that what you call fair sharing of pie? The province of Manitoba, during the same period received accumulated revenues of $78.5 million, and incurred expenditures of $13.4 million. The province's net benefit was thus $65.1
The Budget-Mr. C. Smith
million. Provinces other than Manitoba also received benefits from mining development in my constituency although they did not incur expenditures. The accumulated total of these benefits reached $81 million by the end of 1971. From the foregoing figures it is easy to see how important mining is to northern Manitoba, especially Churchill, and that mining is indeed the economic base of the region.
May I now deal with northern Manitoba's fresh water fishery. I feel that such a fishery could easily employ an additional 150 to 200 Manitoba residents. That is the potential. Many lakes in northern Manitoba are stocked with fresh water fish such as trout, pickerel, whitefish and so on. The federal government has become involved in the marketing of fresh water fish in Manitoba. I am not convinced that the board is doing the job for which it was established, for the simple reason that a bureaucracy has become involved in the handling, processing and sale of this fish. I feel that the government should establish a standing committee of this House on the fresh water fisheries of Canada, which should be separate and distinct from the committee which deals with the salt water fisheries, as I do not think the fresh water fishery of Canada has been given adequate attention.
May I now touch on transportation in Churchill. I do not think any part of the country can be developed properly unless it is served by a good transport system. Northern Manitoba at present is served by a railway and a form of road. Our overland transport systems are limited. Basically, the area is served by aircraft. Aircraft are the only means of transport for isolated communities.
The airport at Thompson, Manitoba, is being used beyond capacity because of overcrowding to the point at which it is unsafe to land aircraft or fly passengers out from there. In July, the airport handled 5,200 landings; it is handling, on average, 4,000 landings per month. We acquired a new control tower at the airport, however, as air transport is vitally important to my constituency, I feel that the expanded facilities requested by municipal authorities and the town fathers should be made available. I submit that the government should consider expanding these facilities immediately.
I wish to register a complaint concerning the Air Transport Board. As aircraft are so important in meeting our transport needs, I suggest that changes in procedure are required if we are to licence aircraft properly so that they may carry passengers and freight. In some cases carriers have had to wait up to eight months to have their applications processed by the Air Transport Board. Such delays constitute gross neglect on the part of the government, especially as aircraft are so important in developing northern areas which rely almost totally on aircraft as a means of transport.
I also wish to voice a complaint concerning television in the riding I represent, and I do not intend to make anyone feel that I have anything against French-speaking people. Lastt week in Flin Flon a notice appeared stating that the CRTC would hold a hearing in Montreal on December 10 to have a second television channel in The Pas and Flin Flon. This second channel will be French. It will be a rebroadcast from CBWFT St. Boniface. The people in Flin Flon were appalled at the notice appearing in the paper

The Budget-Mr. Raines
with no consultation whatsoever with the people of Flin Flon or The Pas, especially when Flin Flon and The Pas combined have a population of only 8 per cent whose mother tongue is French. There are many people whose mother tongue is French; however, their children neither speak nor understand French.
I understand the cost is to be an initial $78,000, plus operating and rental costs. I wonder whether it would be possible to put this toward a second English channel in my constituency or, with 15,000 Cree Indians in the constituency of Churchill, possibly we could have a second channel in Cree. This would probably make a little more sense.
When talking about inflation, cutting government costs and so on, I wonder how we can justify an expenditure of -this amount for such a small portion of the population. Perhaps this is a policy that has to go ahead and maybe I have no way of stopping it, but there are many people in my constituency who would support a second English channel. I do not believe many will be watching the French network.
The forest resources of the constituency of Churchill are also a very important aspect of our economy. I am sure all members have heard of Churchill Forest Industries. Perhaps everything they have heard has been bad. However, if you visit The Pas, Manitoba, you do not hear too many bad things about it because it has created a lot of jobs for people in northern Manitoba. This is what we have been pressing for, more jobs for the people of the north. We want the people of the north not only to have a place to live, but we want them to call it their home. You cannot develop a home by just coming up there, trying to make a fast buck and leaving. We want people to come there and stay.
The forest resources are going to be depleted if we do not get some help. I plead with the government to provide some help to protect those forest resources. I understand that in Quebec there are several CL 215 water bombers to protect the forests. In Manitoba we have a couple of old Canso aircraft that are not in very good shape. They have been through a few wars. I believe there is now an application from the province of Manitoba to have two CL 215's for forest protection during the summer. I have worked for the forestry department for years, and I certainly support the request for the two CL 215's.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of my first speech as a member of this distinguished assembly allow me, at the outset, to express appreciation for your role. It is, as we all know, a most difficult one.
I also congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for presenting a most commendable budget. I am particularly pleased by the minister's commitment to restrain growth in government expenditures and his proposals to reduce personal income tax, protect savings and sustain capital investments. I am sure these proposals are welcomed not only by my constituents, but by all Canadians.
I wish to pay tribute to those who represented Burnaby-Seymour in past parliaments, most notably the Hon. Ray Perrault who served so well as the federal representative

of this riding from 1968 to 1972. He set high standards, and a tradition of service which I will do my best to live up to, Mr. Speaker.
There is much to be done in Burnaby-Seymour. This is a riding where we see the need for many essential services. Railway overpasses and rapid transit are yet to be provided. We are part of a metropolitan area. There is one point I would like to stress. Our LIP allocations in Burnaby-Seymour are serving two significant purposes, taking people off welfare and unemployment insurance, and providing aid to a great number of noteworthy social and environmental projects. There is much yet to be done in Burnaby-Seymour and in Canada, and I share the expressed eagerness to get on with the job.
In the House of Commons on October 2 of this year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) called for a major reform of parliamentary procedure if liberty and democracy are to survive. I would also like to see a major reform in order that I may survive.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To say that I have been appalled at the time-consuming procedures this parliament must go through to accomplish anything is putting it mildly. While I, perhaps, could accustom myself to juggling my time so that I may be in three or four different places at one time for a 10, 12 or 14 hour day, and in many cases a seven day week, I agree that there must be a better way.
It was suggested that we abandon outmoded ideas so that parliament could express the will of the people efficiently and completely. The proposals for reform included, among other things, strict limits on debates of non-controversial bills, television cameras in parliament, and the exploration of other modern ideas such as electronic voting. I hope that since we are now living in a very fast-paced world, my colleagues will not wish to remain saddled with government machinery of a bygone age.
There is one change that gives me great hope and optimism. That is the fact that television cameras will be allowed in the House of Commons early next year. Once the public gets a picture of the procedures under which the government of Canada must labour-the unwieldy, cumbersome and time-consuming procedures-I think there will be no problem in getting public approval for reform, indeed, public demand for reform.
The Prime Minister outlined a series of proposals to speed legislation through parliament, and he hoped that "members of parliament would give at least an expression of support". Today I want to go on record in wholehearted support of these proposals.
It is in the exploration of other modern ideas that I am most interested, especially in the matter of using some of our communication machinery, with the co-operation of parliament and the public, to help unite Canada, to expedite the business of governments, to keep Ottawa in touch with the people and to bring together in matters of mutur-al interest the municipal, provincial and federal governments.
It is for this reason that I feel it is urgent in the extreme that the federal authorities retain full control of the communications systems in Canada. Some provinces have
November 21, 1974

been asking for jurisdiction over cable television, but I feel most strongly that to ensure that broadcasting remains in the national interest, control must remain a federal concern.
If federal control of cable television is lost it could mean the balkanization and fragmentation of Canada. The BNA Act has already separated us in many ways, but I believe that with a strong federal authority to guarantee the national interest, and with good communication and good will between the various levels of government and the people, many difficulties can be overcome.
To illustrate the need for a direct link of communication and co-operation between Ottawa and the provinces let me mention one problem now in the field of education. Because of the BNA Act education is a provincial matter, and each province has its own standards and requirements. In our extremely mobile society many students face difficulty in moving from one province to another, and university students generally lose credits if they transfer from one Canadian university to another. I feel that students should be able to transfer freely across Canada from one accredited university to another without losing credits.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If anything, it is my opinion that because they are experiencing and learning in new environments and coping with new ways and cultures they should gain credits. This is a question which would require co-operation between all the provinces, and a strong link of communication between Ottawa and the provinces could expedite the matter.
Communication is the key. The complexity of modern problems and the need to solve them quickly is going to require parliament to have a forum in a communications system which will receive and send information to the provinces, a system which will strengthen Canadian unity, a system which will not only seek and find answers from a limitless fund of information, from the most enlightened minds, but will receive and distribute vital information to every part of Canada.
These are only a few things that cable television could do, and because cable could become the principal vehicle of broadcasting to Canadians it is vital to keep it in federal hands. Meanwhile Canada has a national system of broadcasting-the CBC. And with some prodding, the CBC may, like Rip Van Winkle, waken to find itself in today's world. I would like to see the CBC gear itself to new and high demands, because the CBC could be a bridge to unite Canada more than the Canadian Pacific Railway lines united Canada in the past. The CBC could educate, stimulate, create understanding and appreciation of different cultures, places and problems.
The potential of the CBC is boundless, but it must come out of its torpor, its housekeeping bureaucracy. It needs, like any creative enterprise, constant changes and infusions and nourishment. I do not think the CBC has had many changes, infusions or nourishment to speak of for a long time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the past the CBC has had its moments of brilliance. But it has a great deal to answer for, Mr. Speaker. British Columbia and the other provinces-I might say, all of Canada except Toronto-have been shamefully neglected on the national scene. It is a fact that Canadian talent generally has had to go south of the border, or to England or Europe, to gain any recognition or have a chance to perform.
The CBC has failed to create mutual understanding of the French and English viewpoints, when it should have been obvious that the two cultures could have been introduced to each other gradually with diplomacy, tact and humour.
Today, in spite of the fact that it has been forced to devote a certain percentage of time to Canadian content, the CBC seems unable to provide Canadians with the creative outlet we so badly need and want. In any Canadian city, any Canadian small town, any rural community, you will find talent that should be on radio or television. Yet the picture I receive on my set consists of reruns, empty and soul-less movies from the United States, and sports.
Where is there any suggestion of a search for a better world? Where is the vision that should be expressing itself in songs and plays? Where is the attempt to explain and interpret British Columbia to the rest of Canada, the west to the east, and the north to the south? The CBC has a lot of catching up to do. It must become a dynamic outlet for Canadian talent and energies, a force for making things better in Canada.
Summing up, Mr. Speaker, I repeat my support for parliamentary reform. I believe it was Nietzsche who said, "Any truth lasts for only 20 years". And governments, like people, should be continually appraising and rethinking ways and means of achieving their priorities and goals. I urge this parliament to retain jurisdiction over the Canadian communications system, including cable television, and to make new and high demands of our national broadcasting system.
I ask all hon. members to consider the brave new world that our new miracles of communication could bring about. The potential for useful exchange of information, carried across Canada and with other countries, is boundless. We have the machinery, we have the hardware. Now, all we must do is to remember the philosophy which admonishes us "to make no small plans-they have no power to stir men's minds."
