subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the timing of this budget is somewhat different from those of the past six years that I have been here. I do not think it is

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
an anti-climax to suggest that we are now facing a real recession for the first time in six years, though many other countries in the world may be facing a depression.
In Washington, President Ford has finally agreed that the United States economy is winding down and a recession is present. It is interesting to compare President Ford's policy with the policy brought in by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), which is entirely different from the measures taken in the United States as well as different from what the British, under the Labour government, have introduced for their country.
President Ford appears to be sitting tight, with no basic change in policy for the present. His policy is to let business run flat, even to take a slight downturn, so as to cool off prices. He wants to squeeze inflation out of the economy even if it means a recession; he is afraid that unless inflation is conquered it could well double when business recovers. The assessment of business in the United States seems to be for a continued slowdown for the rest of this year, and perhaps into May and June of next year. There is substantial evidence in the United States that prices are rising less quickly.
The budget of the Minister of Finance is quite inflationary. He claimed the other night that he was avoiding the risk of uncontrollable inflation and, at the other end of the stick, the risk of a serious recession and massive unemployment, which he assured us was inhuman. Thus he told us he would take a middle course in order to assure a good economic performance.
What do some of the people who make economic forecasts say about this budget? Mr. Beigie of the C. D. Howe Research Institute says that he is increasingly skeptical and concerned about Canadian policies dealing with inflation, especially now that Canadian inflation has become cost-push, caused, with a few important exceptions, by higher costs rather than by a situation of too much money chasing too few goods. He says that Canada seems to be adopting the view that its inflation problem will be cured by the United States exporting the anti-inflationary effects of a United States recession.
Mr. Beigie went on to say that such an approach assumes fairly close parallels between the economies of our two countries, especially as regards wages, but that those parallels do not in fact exist. The United States labour movement has accepted wage increases so low as to result in an actual decline in the real income of workers. Canadian labour, he says, has not done this. Canadian wages have risen faster, and the wage gap has narrowed between our countries without corresponding changes in productivity.
What has the minister done to control inflation? He has had some flattering suggestions, such as that the government "reconcile the various competing interests in our society," that there be a "national consensus comprising self-discipline" and a "good measure of political courage." The minister is courageously going to have a deficit on national accounts of $1.5 billion in 1975-76. The forecast in May was for a deficit of $160 million. The inflationary gains made by the government now show there is a $250 million surplus. Surely this indicates that through the government's inflation-generating tax collection agencies there will be much more money put into the economy than

was the case six months ago. Even the Minister of Finance admitted this when he stated last May that his 1974-75 financial requirements were estimated at more than $2 billion. These requirements are now only $1 billion, which is a reflection of increased government revenues derived through inflation. This is the effect inflation has had on the government. Government costs have increased. The government, however, is the big winner in the inflation lottery.
While there has been unemployment of over 5 per cent there is a great increase in job vacancies. The government is unwilling to look at the effect unemployment insurance and other measures have had on the number of applicants for positions in the labour force. There is no doubt that there is a need to examine the effect of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and other agencies in order to discern whether the fairly high unemployment rate and the large number of job vacancies are an indication of malfunctioning of the labour market.
There is one aspect of the budget which, while in itself it is not large, yet it is part of what I believe to be an unhealthy way of creating savings. I refer to the possibility of saving $1,000 a year before tax, in respect of buying a house if the money is used for this purpose. This is a laudable objective but it certainly creates distortions with regard to savings. It is agreed that savings are necessary if our economy is to function. However, it has become increasingly obvious that our economy is not functioning well when provision must be made for pre-tax savings in order to generate enough capital. That is one of the great difficulties concerning our economy.
Long ago the government introduced the retirement savings plan and pre-tax deductions with regard to employee pension plans. The government now intends to introduce the home ownership assistance plan, as well as the exemption of tax on the first $1,000 of interest and dividend income. We have had the indexing of many of our pension plans. All of this is creating what I think will be quite an intolerable situation.
We continue to accept a tax system which is basically pitched against savings and in favour of spending. The most revealing aspect of this situation is to be found in the extent to which the generation of savings, employment, financing and economic growth is becoming dependent on the government's willingness to defer taxes. The economy should be capable of generating sufficient savings after taxes to finance both continued renewal and continued growth. By this standard the Canadian economy is in trouble and inflation exacerbates the condition.
Much of inflation is directly attributable to the rapid rise in government spending, and the capacity of the tax system to generate government revenues at rates consistently in excess of what was projected. The long-term implications of a system whereby savings for investment are becoming realizeable only to the extent which our government is prepared to defer taxes on current income, registered retirement and savings plans, a plan of this type of home ownership and equity investment, are admissions that the tax system is too onerous. It can be said that Canadians have cause to worry over the budget. It is now
November 21, 1974

generally conceded that Canada will be lucky to reach 4 per cent real growth in the next year.
There is nothing in the budget to contain inflation. The government apparently is content to allow the United States recession to spill over and act as a restraining influence on Canadian influence. We now have real cost-push inflation. United States unions are accepting much lower increases than are Canadian unions. They are even accepting increases which represent less than the actual cost of living so that the workers receive less real income than previously.
In Canada, on the other hand, we had a settlement in the neighbourhood of 60 per cent in respect of the grainhan-dlers' dispute, and similarly at the Lakehead the grainhan-dlers are asking all that was received in Vancouver, plus a good deal more. Government spending is out of hand. There is no evidence in this budget that the government is involved in any kind of curtailment of its own cash requirements. In the next year it is widely forecast that food costs will rise and will be one of the main inflationary factors, but there is absolutely nothing in the budget to help the farmers produce more food.
Mr. Bruce Whitestone, writing in the Kitchener-Water-loo Herald Record had this to say:
... there is increasing awareness of the likelihood of a business slump. Both rhetorically and actually, thus, anti-inflation policies have been accorded a secondary position.
The main aims of the budget, stimulating the economy to resume its growth and produce jobs and to convince the nation, especially the business community, that it is being done responsibly, are unlikely to be achieved.
A great deal of emphasis is placed on increasing supply as a means to combat inflation. Aside from the dubious validity of this approach, the food sector has been all but ignored by this budget.
Vet, food costs have risen more than any other sector of our economy with the exception of energy prices, and there is every prospect that food prices will be the single biggest inflationary factor in 1975.
No steps were proposed to assist farmers with easier credit or to encourage them to cultivate new land. Similarly, livestock producers received no encouragement from this budget.
At the political level, Mr. Turner is up against a central question of contemporary political economy. The commitment to full or nearly-full employment entails inflation sooner rather than later to a rate which erodes purchasing power faster than the government can augment increases. This time around, the budget does not grapple with this key question.
I think this is one of the great problems in respect of this budget.
Now I wish to turn the subject of the taxation of the resource industries of this country, particularly oil and gas. It is perhaps fortunate, at least for western Canada, that there happens to be oil and gas in that part of Canada. I think the treatment of these resources is of paramount importance to the unity of this country and to the form of Confederation.
If this taxation is mishandled we may well see serious if not fatal strains on the confederate structure of Canada. Western Canada has always felt alienated from the rest of the country, but since the days of Louis Riel strong forces have been at work to tie the west to central Canada, and to make it desirable, if at times unpleasant and unremunerative, for western Canada to be a part of the country's confederation.
The Budget-Mr. Ritchie
Western Canada is not old in the settled sense. It was settled in the beginning by people from Ontario and people from the United Kingdom in the early years, followed by the massive immigration of central Europeans. The single common element which bound together this heterogenous group of people was the British tradition of government, institutions and the Crown. However, in recent years these British institutions have all but disappeared as Ottawa has attempted to establish a sort of distinctly Canadian identity. But western Canadians are not able to take part in this identity. They feel estranged from the symbols and the institutions of central Canada. I think the adoption of the maple leaf in Canada's flag is an example. The maple, as such, is not present in the largest part of the land mass of Canada, certainly not in western Canada. It is a peculiarly central and southern Canadian symbol.
Similarly the attempt to disassociate the British symbols of the Crown and the royal attachment has tended to cut adrift the traditional symbols of the west with which westerners could identify. Up until a few years ago while westerners may have been dissatisfied with confederation largely they regarded themselves as protestors. They hoped that by making their voices heard by blocs of votes they would rectify some of their grievances. This was the main motivation behind the agrarian revolt of 1921, the rise of the Progressive Party, followed in the depression years of the 1930's with the splinter parties, the CCF and Social Credit. But until recent years those who might have favoured some sort of independence or remoteness from the government of Ottawa were not many and were considered local autonomists. Recently there has grown up a great doubt on the part of many western Canadians concerning the value of association with confederation. They cannot be dismissed as crackpots or irresponsible people.
In recent years the finding of natural resources in the west, and the fact that through much of the world small countries are as happy or happier than their largest neighbours all have given rise to a desire for more independence for the west, and at least for a variation of the structure of confederation. I think if we should ignore this, we would do so at our peril. The imposition of the taxes on the oil and gas industries will have a horrendous effect on the economy of the west and its future development.
The desire of the government to have a much lower price for oil within Canada than the world price, for an undetermined length of time, is placing great strains on western credibility. It is all the more senseless when it is realized that the cheap supply of oil and gas in western Canada is very limited and will last a few years at the most. Not only will this action of the federal government make for extremely bad relations with the provinces and with the west, but almost certainly it will lead to a shortage of gas and oil that will make us more dependent on offshore oil. Gone now are the halcyon days when we could expect cheap oil and gas from the tar sands in Alberta.
The minister stated that Ottawa would reduce its share of the tax by his abatement of 10 per cent of the provincial tax, and would further reduce it by a resource profit abatement which, for 1974, would be 10 per cent, for 1975,
1550

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin
12 per cent, and for 1976 and the year thereafter, 15 per cent. This means that the net 1976 federal tax rate will amount to 25 per cent. In the oil economics of today, this means that in 1976 the federal tax rate would be 25 cents a barrel less than it is today.
The minister also lessened the tax for exploration expenditure and depletion allowance. But in not allowing royalties to be a traditional deductible business expense he has reversed a principle of confederation. If Ottawa is to move in such a wholesale fashion with regard to one provincial jurisdiction, what about all the provincial jurisdictions?
This headlong confrontation with the provinces can only spur the provinces to protect their rights as best they can. They could use provincial Crown corporations which have traditionally been exempt from taxation at the federal level. The Minister of Finance stated in his budget that any province which sought to nationalize industry and thereby capture the revenues for itself should think about it carefully, because in such cases the federal government would have to consider the taxation of such Crown corporations.
This statement smacks of a direct desire of the administration to club the Conservative government of Alberta in particular, to conquer the westerners once more and take their resources from them. It is all the more important to westerners considering the great troubles they encountered, to assume control of resources in the 1920s, since on joining confederation they were not allowed to consider their resources as being under their own jurisdiction but had to bargain for them.
The hydro industry has been taken over by the different provincial governments. The minister could have attempted another approach. He could have attempted to work out with the provinces what the definition of royalties should be, and how much they should be taxed. He should have worked out with the provinces at what level royalties could remain deductible for income tax purposes. The government can take that matter to the Supreme Court, but it seems likely that in view of the makeup of the Supreme Court and the appointment of the Chief Justice, the decision will be favourable to the federal government. But, in the long run, the provinces will have to throttle back oil and gas production and in that way eventually natural shortages will force prices up to world levels.
There is another part of the resource industry which has not been touched upon, and that is mining. The mining people are caught in the dispute between Ottawa and Alberta, and this affects all provincial jurisdictions. This budget is dangerous because, for the first time, it has led to a collision between our two main forms of government. The existence of confederation is at stake, and this problem must be resolved if peace in this country is to be achieved.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take part in this budget debate and this, for a number of reasons. One of the main reasons is that it is taking place in historical circumstances, when world events are steeped in uncertainty. In view of these circumstances, this may very well be the
most important budget speech in the history of Canada. Besides, the minister himself indicated nearly openly his concern for and helplessness about our economy which is deteriorating due to increasingly stronger pressures. Moreover, as a desperate shift, he seems to attribute to international forces the responsibility for the future of the Canadian people.
Madam Speaker, I shall explain myself later on this matter, but I want to emphasize first of all that my remarks will be bearing the stamp of objectivity, while setting out as equitably as possible everything which appears to me to be abnormal or inconsistent in the measures proposed by the minister.
First of all, I intend to discuss the main points of the budget speech and, in particular, some of the minister's proposals. Later on, I shall discuss the international situation, to which the minister addresses the thrust of the current debate. I want to show that the picture he has drawn up is far from complete, and that the minister has failed to mention some extremely important factors.
As a whole, the present budget contains proposals which are sound basically. One might, at first glance, be tempted to endorse them. Still, those measures must be analyzed carefully, and criticized in the light of the imperatives dictated by the context in which we now live. Only on that condition can we really judge, in the final analysis, of the value of the budget.
With regard to the minister's proposals on personal income tax, I must say that they are sound generally, and I recognize that they are well founded. Madam Speaker, I even congratulate the minister in this regard. Still, I can reproach him one small thing: they come too late for us to hope for any marked beneficial effects.
As we know, Madam Speaker, when a sick person has urgent need of a doctor, the latter's arrival is beyond value. But when the patient is already dead, or when he has reached the point of no return, the doctor's arrival is really of very little importance. This is how the personal income tax measures strike me.
As the very moment when those measures are announced the benefits provided by them are already reduced by the increase in the cost of living and the inflation now facing this country.
The minister is perfectly right in also taking credit for reducing to 5 per cent the tax on building materials. We have been urging him to do just that for already a couple of years. Three or four years ago I was saying: let us do away completely with that tax to ensure a true respite in construction, but nothing was done. Now, after the situation has deteriorated, the minister accepts in part our proposal. That step will provide some help but a lot less effectively in the present context. Had it been adopted when we proposed it it would have its full effect today. Construction would have been a lot more active. That is a sector that affects a very large number of workers from the lumberjack, the trades, and others, without forgetting all the industries that participate in the construction industry.

November 21, 1974

On the one hand, there would have been less unemployment and, on the other, Canadians would have been better prepared financially to meet the inflationary increase that we had and have to meet. That would have been seeing ahead, and at the same time the government would have prevented the drop that now worries it about the number of housing starts. But it seems clearly to me now that those measures which would have been fine before are now quite secondary because they come too late.
Personal income tax reductions, the lowering of the sales tax on building materials, the $500 grant for a year by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to any new owner of a new house, all those measures and most of the others mentioned in the budget all have the same flaw in that they come too late. If those important steps had been taken earlier Canadians would have found themselves in a position where they could get out of it, as will do in the months to come our big oil and mining companies that the minister did everything to protect. The minister himself said in his budget that he had gone out to meet those big companies and examine the situation.
He then wanted to include in the budget some measures allowing big companies to buckle themselves against market conditions while, to use his own words, providing a fair return to their shareholders. If the minister is doing such a good thing in granting special measures to large corporations, so that they can make profits, would it not have been also advisable for him to give farmers, old people, low income citizens and rental housing builders, before inflation shaves their savings, a chance to lighten their tax burden before tonight or the budget speech, to help them keep afloat and provide their budget with a fair return?
Madam Speaker, as far as the aged are concerned, the minister proposed measures aimed, as he said, at protecting savings from the effects of inflation. At first glance, it seems an excellent and comprehensive measure. However, on closer examination, the picture changes completely. It might well be that the minister wants to protect savings and indeed that could help some people.
But such is not the real problem for most aged persons, but it is rather the need of a minimum vital income. This is not a true but rather a negative form of assistance. It is not bad, but it only affects the people who already enjoy some security. But the others, majority, those who have little more than the old age pension, what do they become? Indeed, in many cases, only one spouse old age security due to the age difference. The minister does not refer to them. It is very well to protect the savings of the aged, but who will protect those who are penniless? Such is the question. This is why we say that we can consider with derision those measures meant to help the elderly. There would be much to say about the matter, but I will come back to it later.
There is another point, Madam Speaker, which I must raise. Alone, it would justify a bitter objection against that budget and it is the fact that nowhere in the minister's speech reference is made to agriculture. This is most serious in my opinion. I am against it not only because I represent a strongly rural constituency, but also because I know full well that strong agricultural action was expect-
The Budget-Mr. Beaudoin
ed at this time by all Canadians that share a real awareness of the situation.
A number of countries around the world are hit by starvation. Our grain reserves are almost nonexistent. We face serious problems concerning our egg, poultry and beef producers. Our people leave their farms while population is growing. A growing number of farmers have to go bankrupt or leave their farms. They realize more than ever their production costs are not even covered by the price at which they sell their goods. And finally, if they sell their farms to others than their sons, in comes federal income tax that takes almost everything they get for their farms, animals machinery, chattels and what have you.
At the same time our gracious and smiling Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) proposes in this House a budget almost completely devoid of anything for our farmers, as if they were non-entities.
Some things are not clear to me. Consumers know that food prices now reach astronomical levels. Farmers know they cannot make ends meet and produce at normal costs. Finally, everyone knows from the budget speech that the Canadian government cares nothing about it.
On the other hand, the minister places much hope in international relations based on the goodwill of the countries to solve the current economic crisis. I am tempted to say to him, "Mr. Minister, you should take immediate steps to prevent your budget speech from being known to other countries." If he does not, he simply risks losing their confidence, and even being considered blind.
The minister says in his speech he has much hope on close international consultation. He even points to sharing with nations in trouble, and further states:
Do we not have an even greater duty to conserve food in a starving world?
And during all that time in his budget he does not say a word about the farmer. And in the same speech, there is not a word about agriculture which is slowly going down the drain in front of everybody's eyes. Where is the logic? Where do we find responsibility in that? I would even go so far as to say: Where is the goodwill so necessary to correct the world situation for those who are hungry, for those who are hungry even in our country?
Canada, through its Minister of Finance, has made certain commitments to help other countries, in the agricultural field for example, and at the same time we are letting our own agricultural situation deteriorate without making a move. How will that be considered by the nation's concerned? They will have proof positive that Canada is ready to promise them anything without ever intending to deliver. Won't that just be one more good old example in humanity's history where everybody talks while nothing is done to correct an already rotten situation.
Madam Speaker, I would now like to say a word about the international situation that the Minister of Finance considers of the utmost importance to correct a situation.
With the economic corridor the government and its Minister of Finance are now entering, and for months to come, the Canadian nation is being exposed to taking on the immediate colour that very short-term world events will give it. On the other hand, this turn of events on the international stage is very closely related to the world
28543-30%

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Condon
energy crisis and the minister indicates that the uncertainty he feels towards the future is linked to the burning and explosive question of oil.
But we may very shortly have, to take into account another factor, just as important as oil, if not more, and I would like the minister to pay attention to it, for I noticed he made no mention of it in his speech. If he did so on purpose, then he was simply confessing that he knows of no better solution. On the other hand, if he does not take it into account, we might have a whale of a surprise. I am talking about an element which possibly vouches for an even worse world situation than the oil conflict, I mean the raw materials rush.
The budget speech may be the most dramatic ever heard, not so much because of what it says, as because of some disputable points and the serious situation it hints at, and above all because it is an acknowledgment by our government of its inability to cope-even timidly-with our present difficulties. The objective outlined in it is simply to keep the country afloat and wait. Several of the suggested measures are worthwhile, but they have come too late to be successful. This is not a creative, dynamic budget which aims at initiating things, but rather a feedback budget. It is therefore an indication that the government is holding up any initiative, taking a defensive stand, and waiting for developments before it moves, and that it is relying to a considerable extent on positive changes in the world situation.
The government has already waited too long, in my opinion, to take national measures. It is waking up now, but it is too late. And the only possible solution, as we have seen, is a status quo budget which betrays a form of weakness, even if at first sight it may appear as a form of administrative flexibility.
What will now happen in Canada depends no longer on what we do according to the minister himself, but on whether or not the international situation changes for the better. But past experience as concerns the results achieved by international organizations makes us wonder what will happen. I do not wish to be an alarmist, but we must be realistic. The opening attitude of the minister, as the rest of his budget speech, shows that he no longer has any choice. All depends on the possibility of changes on an international or national level. He has little or no control over our future.
The control that we expected the minister to announce, the control of our economy, either has been forgotten or is beyond the minister's capacity. He feels that the government is unable to establish this control. The Speech from the Throne already gave indication of a strongly anticipated crisis because of the international economic situation, and the budget speech now confirms this.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, a great honour has been done me. I am speaking for the first time in parliament, and I have been asked to speak on the budget. To be honest, I am overwhelmed to see the tremendous crowds everywhere, to see all those members of parliament who are diligently paying attention, listening, and hanging on my every word.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Their attentiveness is the criterion of Canadian people in action. It is important for the people of this country to know just how diligently members of parliament work in the interests of those whom they represent. Frankly, I was surprised to note how much work members do. I do not think the people back in our constituencies realize just how hard members work, how many hours they put in when they are away from home. They can only know this if they come to Ottawa and perhaps follow a member around for one day.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just during the daytime.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am grateful for the way new members have been accepted in Ottawa. The attentiveness and helpfulness of staffs, including the staff of this House, cannot be praised too highly. All have been kind to the boy away from home in the big city.
We belong to a special club, and the honour of belonging to it is something no one can take away from us. Our children, grandchildren and even great grandchildren will cherish the knowledge that at one time we, of this House, had our names on the side of a desk in the House of Commons.
I said I come from a small town. I come from Strathroy, where I served as mayor for three terms. But I am not just a small town boy; I come also from that great city which returned three great members to this House, all of whom sit on my side; I come from Verdun, Quebec.
I am fortunate to be here, being the third Liberal member since confederation to be given the honour of representing the riding now known as Middlesex-London-Lambton. I follow in the footsteps of impressive men, Mr. Robert McCubbin and Mr. Jim Lind, who have set an example I shall try to follow in the next several years.
We must remember that the budget affects people. Too often we forget that the politician who is closest to the people is not the one at the federal or provincial level, but the one at the local level. I shall try to be as close to my people now that I am a member of parliament as I was when I was mayor of Strathroy.
The budget contains important provisions which will affect sewers and storm sewers. Of course one does not go around shouting how happy one is to see storm sewers. Nevertheless, they are important for the growth of Canada, important for the growth of towns, and important for housing developments. We need more houses. The federal government has said, through the medium of the budget, that it will make money available to municipalities and enable them to push ahead with sewer programs. I am sure municipalities will be grateful for this help, as it is difficult for municipalities to use their own financial resources and accumulate enough to pay for these services.
All this shows that the federal government is aware of municipal problems. Too often governments in the past have forgotten about them. I make this point as a former mayor of Strathroy who hopes to grow, through experience, into an effective member of parliament and representative of Middlesex-London-Lambton.
November 21, 1974

Before coming here I was concerned about municipal matters; now, as a member of parliament, I must consider the wider picture which affects all Canada. That is why I say that the budget affects all Canadians. It is not designed for separate groups. It is time Canadians forgot regionalism. If we want to grow into a respected world power under the leadership of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), we must forget regionalism. I see some young people in the gallery; they know what I am talking about. They think of themselves first as Canadians, and they know the correctness of what I say more than some others in this chamber.
The budget, as I say, is for the benefit of all Canadians, including those who were not given the opportunities which you and I were given, Madam Speaker. We are obligated to help unfortunate people. If we do not, we shall not fulfil our obligations to those who are not as fortunate as ourselves. We must send food to the needy. Again, we are obligated to do this, not because we are Canadians, or politicians, but because we owe unfortunate people something-and because we have had it so damned good ourselves. This obligation, as I am sure the opposition will agree, is an ongoing one. So, let us get on with the job. Let us pass the budget, because we have work to do on behalf of the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have listened very carefully to the remarks of the previous speaker and he stated that the constituency of Verdun has had three representatives from the government party. However, we must not forget that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) has also been the representative of Verdun, and I would not want the hon. member to forget it as he was a Liberal at that time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make a few comments this evening in relation to the budget, as well as to other matters occurring in the country which are of much concern to me. I think it would be fair to say that at this time the most obvious concern to me and all Canadians is the question of national unity. It is more than a coincidence that since this administration has been in power, unity within the country has been suffering in one way or another.
We started in 1968 with what appeared to be a tremendous strain on unity as a result of the method by which this administration was carrying out its bilingualism policies. It did so in a very insensitive way without concern for the various regions of the country.
Even though the intention may have been to increase unity, it in fact spread much disunity in the country. The record since that time has not improved. It has been very much the same. I can quite easily point out many examples where unity has been very much strained by this particular administration.
Let us take a look at government policies concerning relations between the federal and provincial governments, particularly relations between the federal government and some western provinces. I can be even more specific and say Alberta. About a year or so ago, when it appeared-
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should speak on the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My friend has not been here very long. If he has, he has been sleeping most of the time. He is one of those Quebec members who sleep most of the time. If he had been awake, he would realize that during the budget debate the subjects can be very far ranging simply because the budget speech touches on almost every aspect of Canadian life. Therefore in the debate it is quite reasonable to touch on a number of subjects. I am sure Your Honour is aware of all this, but I say it for the edification of the hon. member who is new to the game and needs to be educated on procedure.
I want to deal with some of the other things that are creating disunity in this country. These factors of disunity are not occurring by accident. They are occurring by design. For example, a year ago the federal government decided to bring in an export tax on oil. We all know the result of that. There was a strain on the relations between Alberta and this government, simply because there was no consultation with that provincial government prior to that move being instituted.
There was then an allocations bill which tramped over provincial rights. It was conceived and put forward without any consultation with the provinces involved. We now have before the House the petroleum administration bill which does essentially the same. It tramps over provincial rights. It was conceived, produced and put forward without any significant consultation with the provinces involved.
During the recent election campaign there was a blatant and open attack on the province of Alberta by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). He committed something like 17 per cent of Alberta's petroleum supply to a particular plant in Ontario without even so much as a telephone call to Alberta, the province which, under the constitution, is responsible for the development of these resources and, indeed, is the owner of them.
We can look at the relationship between the federal government and the maritime provinces insofar as provincial rights are concerned, with regard to offshore minerals. The same has happened there. In short, what we are seeing is a federal government that is involving itself in an open power struggle to take more and more authority unto itself.
We should look for the reasons why the government feels it must have all this authority.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They were elected by the people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think we can come up with a reasonable answer. I heard a comment from the member opposite, who seems to be still awake, that they were elected by the people. I ask him who he thinks elected the provincial governments? I ask him what is the meaning of the constitution? Why have a constitution which delineates quite clearly provincial authority and federal authority? Why do we have a federal government encroaching on areas which the constitution gives to the provinces? It

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Yewchuk
must be because the government is power hungry. It has a greed for power.
I am particularly concerned because this power struggle is being led by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I see him as a person who would have done very well as a dictator in the days of old when dictatorships were commonplace. They still are in some places, but they are not commonplace or acceptable in this country. That is something the federal administration fails to realize.
What we are seeing is the result of a failure on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government to achieve constitutional change through the accepted legal channels. In spite of repeated efforts over the past six years there has not been any success in changing the constitution through acceptable channels. Therefore, what we have is a slow but progressive change through the back door. It is a slow but progressive erosion, and invasion into areas which have traditionally been known to be provincial jurisdiction.
I am quite concerned about the technique that is being used in this power struggle, a technique of continuously provoking confrontation. It is rather interesting that last year about this time when we were faced with winter, an effort was made to provoke a confrontation between the province of Alberta and the federal government.
The federal government wanted to pit Alberta against the rest of the country. It tried to provoke Alberta into saying it would cut off oil for the rest of the country. The federal government could then run around the country saying it was the great saviour of the nation-"support us or you will freeze in the dark". That was the attitude the government took last fall and last winter. When spring rolled around the weather improved and there was not such a great hazard. The whole thing subsided. There was not much mention about it. We are now coming into another winter, and the whole thing is being started again through open and repeated provocation in the same manner as before.
If the intention is to provoke Alberta into shutting off supplies of energy I do not think it will succeed, because I believe Alberta is showing greater concern over the national interest than is the federal government. The result of the federal government's attitude is a widening sense of alienation in the west. Westerners are beginning to wonder what will come next-is the federal government planning to end the Crowsnest rates? Is it trying to punish the west for sending back so many Conservatives after the last election?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same number.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is a statement commonly made by federal Liberals after the election campaign of July 8. They say to westerners, "You will find out now what it is like to have no representation in the government". Then we find that a man from the other place, a Senator, has been appointed as spokesman for Alberta.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a member of parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, he is a member of parliament but he happens to be an appointed member, a former bagman for the Liberal party. He did a good job in that capacity, and maybe he can do a good job of advising the government on the feeling in Alberta. However, I think it is fair to say that elected members are in closer contact with their constituents, and therefore in a better position to give advice which would make the government sensitive to the needs of particular segments of our society. This is a correction which should be made forthwith.
Faced with the government's continuing efforts to alter the constitution by the back door rather than through legal means, Canadians are at a crossroads. They have to decide whether they really want this kind of constitutional change or not. In making such a decision they will have to make up their minds whether they believe the present administration, under the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his colleagues, can do a better job of developing the Canadian petroleum industry than the provincial governments which have been entrusted with this task under the constitution. Can they be sure that if the constitution is changed, either by direct or by indirect methods, so as to give the federal government this power, the security of supply we have enjoyed in the past will continue, or that there will be a more effective development of our natural resources?
On the basis of the government's record I am not convinced that it can do a better job of developing these resources than we have seen so far. The result of the federal government's incursions into the energy field so far has simply been the slowing down of exploration and development.
Only this morning we saw a report in the national press concerning a report produced by the National Energy Board which predicts that within four to seven years Canada will no longer be self-sufficient in oil. Mr. Speaker, that is a very short period. Yet in the past year, as a result of federal intervention, we find that important sections of the oil industry are leaving the country and that exploration has been severely restricted.
The development of the tar sands is being retarded; there is a lack of interest because the oil industry is unable to make long term plans, due to the continuing vacillation of the administration in Ottawa. We should consider the possible long term consequences of this interference with the petroleum industry. It may well be we shall be dependent on oil from the Middle East, Venezuela or some other country. I do not think we should get ourselves into such a situation, particularly when we have the capacity to be self-sufficient.
I also wish to comment on the subject of multi-cultural-ism which has been my responsibility recently. Following the 1972 campaign we saw what appeared to be a genuine interest in this subject expressed by the federal government, to the point at which a minister was assigned to the portfolio and a budget was placed at his disposal. This was an occasion for hope among one third of Canada's population. At that period the administration held office only through the support of a shaky minority, and I believe it was more sensitive to the needs of Canadians than either the previous government or the government whose members sit on the treasury benches today.
November 21, 1974

In any case, between 1972 and 1974 some progress appeared to be made and ethnic groups began to believe there was some hope for their survival as identifiable groups. However, after the 1974 campaign one of the first actions to be taken was the removal from office of the minister responsible for this particular area, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz). His post was obliterated as a separate entity.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The demise of the program. Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Responsibility was transferred to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro)-the relationship is difficult to explain. The Prime Minister is now trying to convince us that the Minister of Labour is able to do more for multi-culturalism by devoting 5 per cent of his time to it than the hon. member for Parkdale was able to do by devoting his full time to it. I don't know whether the Prime Minister feels the Minister of Labour is a superman, or whether he has a low opinion of the ability of the hon. member for Parkdale. I hope it is not the latter.
I was quite concerned when the throne speech was read, and even more concerned when the budget speech was read, to find absolutely no mention of the subject of rr ulticulturalism or of any plans to change direction. What we heard was a reiteration that greater priority would be placed on bilingualism. I have no objection to that; I think bilingualism is fine. I am not saying that bilingualism and multiculturalism are not compatible. But I am saying that the failure of the government to make any mention of multiculturalism, while placing a lot of stress on other topics, might lead some Canadians to feel they are once again being suppressed.
I just want to make a few general comments about Canada's ethnic groups and on why we must ensure that we do not suppress multiculturalism. I think it is fair to say that a lot of people came to this country seeking freedom. Whether it be political freedom or economic freedom, generally this was the goal they were seeking; and I think it is also fair to say that these two freedoms were provided them in abundance.
Let me just examine what has happened to these people generally since they arrived in this country. I want to look at them as individuals. These people did well economically, they did well politically, but what happened to them socially? Hon. members can examine any group-Italians, Germans, Ukrainians, Poles. Some have had to change their names for one reason or another; they have changed their original name to an English name. Some of them changed their religion. Others became ashamed to speak their own language, and in some cases refused to acknowledge publicly the language group from which they came.
What does that mean to you, Mr. Speaker? I suggest it means they have experienced very much a lack of freedom in one area, namely, the area of social freedom. These people have been facing all kinds of prejudices in this country, prejudices against their name, their religion and their language. As a result they felt they could not survive or compete in this country unless they became Anglicized or Francophonized. The policies of the government have
The Budget-Mr. Anderson
been reinforcing this feeling. If we want to extend hope to these people-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I regret I must interrupt the hon. member. I have tried to allow him a little extra time to permit him to make his point, but I think he would need more than a few seconds.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am glad to see this budget back before the House again after a long wait since May. It is like the return of the prodigal child-very welcome. I congratulate the minister for the level headed approach that his budget takes toward Canada's economic situation in November of 1974.
Canada's economy is a sound economy. We have withstood the economic unrest that is sweeping the world better than many of our fellow members in the world community. For this reason I am glad to support a budget that pursues a reasonable path between the extremes of excessive government stimulation of the economy on the one hand, and creating a deliberate economic slowdown to combat inflation, on the other hand.
This is not a time for extreme measures but a time for sensible, stable, economic measures. I am equally glad that this is a budget which seeks to protect the most vulnerable of our citizens, those least able to bear the effects of world wide inflation, from erosion of their limited incomes by rising prices. While the amount of the tax cuts proposed in this budget for 1974 and 1975 may seem small to some members of the House, I can assure them that there are many people in the constituency of Comox-Alberni to whom that extra income in the pay envelope means a great deal.
The people of Comox-Alberni are not the wealthiest in Canada, by and large they are hard working folk who put in their shifts in mills and factories, in fishing boats or logging camps, in mines or on farms. They are the strong and enduring foundation of this country's economy, people who work hard for their pay. They do not want a strictly controlled economy. They want to earn their living, to earn enough to maintain a respectable standard of living, and to put by a little from each pay cheque towards their future.
I believe that the proposals contained in this budget will help the people of Comox-Alberni lead the kind of life they want to lead. The tax cuts will enable them to see more of the income they earn go toward providing them with the things that make up a good life. The proposed exemptions of $1,000 in income from their savings will make it that much easier for them to look ahead to the future for which they plan.
One of the problems the people of Comox-Alberni face, a problem faced most by young couples beginning their lives together, is the high cost of housing. For many the cost of purchasing a modest home in which to raise their families is prohibitive. That is why I am pleased to see the proposed reduction of the federal sales tax on building and construction materials. If there is such a thing as the Canadian dream, one of its most primary elements is the desire of each family to own its own home. Any steps taken by the government to help make this wish a reality will not be lightly dismissed. And to make sure that this reduction in the federal sales tax benefits those who most need it, I hope that the government through the proper

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Anderson
agency will ensure that the resulting reduction in the cost of housing is passed on to the consumer.
Comox-Alberni is an island riding, surrounded on three sides by straits and inlets of the Pacific Ocean. Communications and transportation in such a riding, separated as it is by 30 miles of water from the mainland, are of vital concern to its people. For that reason I welcome the budget's proposed elimination of the federal sales tax on transportation equipment. If the elimination of that tax results in lower shipping costs and resultant power prices of consumer goods, as I am sure the government intends, the people of Comox-Alberni will not take it amiss.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, let me describe to you the situation facing the city of Port Alberni, one of the three major centres of population in the northern half of Vancouver Island. Port Alberni is connected to the rest of Canada by one narrow strip of two lane blacktop. A city of nearly 25,000, Port Alberni must import almost every consumer item, from can openers to heavy machinery, by way of that road. And almost everything Port Alberni imports must come by truck along that single highway.
Port Alberni is one of many similar cases in Comox-Alberni constituency. Transportation and communications in such isolated areas as these, despite the fact that they are bustling, growing cities, are matters of great concern to the people who live there. In many of the smaller settlements, however, boat transportation is the only means of moving people and goods. Further 1o the proposed elimination of the sales tax on transportation equipment, I would urge upon the government similar measures for boats and ships where these craft are used as transporters of goods to areas unreachable by roads.
Recently it was reported in the press that people in the Mount Waddington region, the northern part of my constituency, wished to secede from Canada and unite with Alaska. The residents of that area felt that they were not enjoying the full benefits of being Canadians. To relieve the doubts of the people of northern Vancouver Island as to their welcome place among the rest of Canada, and in order to unite this country from coast to coast by one continuous highway, I would urge the government to extend the trans-Canada highway northwards from its present end in Nanaimo to the town of Port Hardy, and from there onwards to the west coast of Vancouver Island.
Not only would this extension of the highway restore the people of the Mount Waddington district to the Canadian fold, it would bring a better quality of life to the more isolated areas through an increased input of goods and materials, along with lower prices because of easier transportation processes. In the same vein, I w ould like to see in the near future the extension of the Canadian Pacific Railway lines northward from their present terminus in the city of Courtenay to the people of the northern end of Vancouver Island.
In villages like Port Alice and Port McNeill the recent announcement that television service will be extended to the people there in 1976 has been received with great happiness. We of the southern regions of Canada, surrounded by the technological wonders of the urban centres, cannot, I believe, truly understand how much a seem-

ingly small thing as television reception can mean to those who are denied it by virtue of their isolation from the mainstream of the country.
Being able to announce that television service would soon be a reality in the northern end of Vancouver Island has been one of the most enjoyable acts I have performed in my short time as a new member of this House. I know that, for those people up there, to be able to sit down and watch the Grey Cup or the Stanley Cup playoffs is not something they take for granted.
Still on the subject of transportation, I would urge the government to examine closely the prospect of improving and developing small craft harbours along the coastline that borders three quarters of the constituency of Comox-Alberni. To many of the people in that riding, boats must take the place of automobiles as the primary means of transportation. To people who must rely on boats to make the weekly shopping trip, to visit a neighbour, even to bus their children to school, proper and well maintained wharves and harbours are as necessary as roads and parking lots are to mainland residents.
Vancouver Island is ready to grow. It has the resources; it has the people; it has the Pacific Ocean, with all the markets of the Pacific Rim, at its doorstep. What Vancouver Island needs is better transportation facilities, in the areas I have outlined, and the establishment of deep sea ports to handle the trade in natural resources that could be emanating from Canada's most westerly territory. The excellent natural harbour in the city of Campbell River, for example, could become an outlet on the Pacific that would help keep Canada's exports steadily on the increase.
Another matter of primary importance to Comox-Alberni is the maintenance of a strong and viable fishing industry on the west coast. Such policies as the establishment of a territorial limit of 200 miles, or to the edge of the continental shelf, can have a real and profound effect on the future of that industry. I would urge the government to pursue strongly this policy of extending Canada's territorial limit, taking into consideration traditional fishing rights of our neighbours, to protect our fishermen from encroachment on their waters.
Another matter which I would very much like to see the government become involved in is the question of establishing a strong coastguard presence on the west coast. If, as is government policy, we are to have the 200-mile limit, the Canadian presence in our territorial waters must be augmented so that our claim to these waters is not just theory but fact.
Additionally, a well established coastguard force, with bases all along the British Columbia coast, would raise the level of protection we can offer to men on the water. A fast, efficient search and rescue capability would seem sufficient reason for creating a coastguard, without taking into account the IR duties in fisheries patrol and customs law enforcement. Another advantage to having a coastguard service on the west coast would be to raise the general level of competence in navigation and seamanship among the men who make their living from the sea. When, as would most likely be the case, members of the coast guard leave the service to work in the fishing industry,
November 21, 1974

their knowledge and experience would serve to make it a safer and more professional enterprise than ever.
I would like to turn to the subject of national defence, a subject that has been commented on in relation to the budget, both here in this House and in the media. From 1956 to 1962 I was proud to wear the uniform of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I was proud to have been adjudged worthy to serve Canada as a member of its armed forces. I am still proud today of having had that distinction.
I urge the government to ensure that those men and women who wear the uniform of the Canadian armed forces today can continue to share my pride. I ask that those people who are willing to lay down their lives for this nation receive the consideration they most assuredly deserve. Let their equipment be the best we can give them, and let their pay be equal to the task we ask of them. The Bible reminds us that the labourer is worthy of his hire; the soldier is no less worthy.
The armed forces of Canada have a reputation all across the world as powerful fighting troops and efficient peacekeepers. I believe that these two roles, so seemingly in contradiction and yet related to each other like two arms of one body, have brought the Canadian armed forces the respect and admiration not only of the military establishments of other nations, but of foreign civilian populations as well. Few nations have matched Canada's forces' reputation both in the field and in the buffer zones, a reputation which I count as a privilege to uphold. I urge the government to give present and future members of our armed forces the opportunity to live up to that reputation.
One other matter I would like to put before this House is a question that concerns not only the people of Comox-Alberni, but all women across Canada. I am referring to the plight of women who through divorce, separation, or widowhood are left with the responsibilities of supporting and caring for a family all by themselves. For many women in this unhappy situation the only course open to them is to rely on social assistance for the support of their families. For many, the cost of day care facilities for their children takes too large a bite out of their incomes, so that they would actually be financially better off on welfare than out earning a living with their skills.
I think it a tragedy that women who want to work, perhaps at jobs that they find worthwhile and fulfilling, must leave the work force in order to give their children a decent standard of living. I ask the government to consider a complete tax exemption for women in these circumstances who are earning a moderate income. Although this measure would admittedly reduce government revenues by some lost taxes, I am certain that the loss would be more than equally offset by the reduction in the cost of maintaining these women and their children through social assistance. Such a measure would also reduce the numbers of the unemployed as well as provide the social benefit of putting skilled people, who want to work, back into the labour force.
I would like to go on record that as a western member I am in agreement with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on his position regarding royalties. It is my sincere opinion that in the province of British Columbia the mining royalties will drive the mining industry out of the province. Already exploration has drastically declined and
The Budget-Mr. McCleave
speculative capital for mining investment has left the province for healthier climates.
The present government of British Columbia can only be called a disaster looking for a catastrophe to happen. It is hard for members of parliament who come from provinces which, I assume, have sane governments, to realize the insanity taking place in la plus belle province.

speechtext: Listen to a true Canadian speaking.

I must apologize for my lack of French. However, in my constituency of Comox-Alberni my constituents have told me that first I should learn to speak English before I learn how to speak French.
B.C. is a part of Canada, although at times it is hard to determine.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Personally I pledge my support for the federal concept which, I believe, is ultimately in the best interest of western Canada and of B.C. in particular.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought the name of the province was British Columbia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In closing, Mr. Speaker, allow me to say again that I congratulate the Minister of Finance on the sensible approach he is taking toward resolving Canada's economic problems in the light of worldwide inflation. I believe that the course the government is pursuing to combat inflation and prevent an economic slump will spare Canada further economic unrest, while at the same time allowing this country to progress to heights that not even we as members of parliament can imagine in our wildest dreams, and this includes of course the province of Alberta.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is probably appropriate that I have only ten minutes in which to make my speech since part of my argument tonight, later on when I deal with the matter of the reform of parliamentary procedures, is to suggest that the House limit itself to ten minute speeches henceforth. I only hope, Sir, that time will permit me to get to that part of my argument, because now I have other things to say.
The first thing I would like to note, out of deference to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who is here this evening, and who has been here to listen to participants in the debate on his budget, is that I will say something about it, although not very much. I think it was an attempt by the minister to adjust to the pressures of inflation by easing the burden on some who suffer from inflation. With the exception perhaps of measures such as the partial removal of the sales tax on construction materials, I do not think that there were many measures in the budget that dealt with the root causes of inflation or tried to take some strong corrective measures.
I think also that it is pretty horrifying when we have two such budget presentations in the year, and suddenly figures that the minister forecasts are seven or eight

November 21, 1974
The Budget-Mr. McCleave
figures apart from the same forecast made a few months earlier. If that does not indicate how deeply the fangs of inflation are biting, then nothing else does.
I am a native of Moncton, New Brunswick, and one of the proud things that happened to that city this summer was when a group of young singers-an Acadian group- went to the United Kingdom and, in competition with some of the great choirs from all over the world, gained not one prize but four international prizes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think that is an event that is worthy of being put on the record in the House. It is one of the things that make me proud of having been born in Moncton.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I can deal with many things here this evening. I am a philosophical fellow. When I come here in the morning and look down the corridor, and see that the other place has a different floor wax than the one that is used here, I am inclined to ask whether there could not be some saving in combining the services in this House and the other place. God knows, sir, what battles are fought in the middle of the night, jurisdictional battles by the ladies armed with wax mops, as to who draws the other place's wax line and who does the waxing for this part of the building. Anyway, there is room for savings here and I hope both Mr. Speaker and Madam Speaker of the other place can get together and perhaps work out some joint services.
During the election campaign something different happened to me, something that was a challenge. I asked the deaf community in Halifax and East Hants to attend one of my political rallies. It is quite something to stand up and try to tell a joke, as perfectly as I tell them, and to have it translated by a person through sign language with her hands. Yet these people enjoyed being brought into the political swim. If any member in his or her next campaign wants to have a different type of experience, and a satisfying one, just ask the deaf community to attend meetings and they will find there is a great deal of enjoyment in it.
I would like to make one plea for people who are disabled in this way. I would like to see every deaf person have the right to a special machine that can be attached to the telephone. I think its cost is $200 or less. It lights up to indicate that someone is trying to contact that person. There is also a special typing apparatus that is able to transmit messages back and forth. I think that is a small amount of money for a very substantial help to disadvantaged citizens.
Later on in the session I will be dealing with some of the local issues, but now my time is running out and I would like to turn to some of the affairs as they concern the Chair of the House of Commons. I would ask you, Sir, to compliment Mr. Speaker on his selection. On election night, given the realities as they existed in the province of Ontario, I turned to my wife and said: "I bet that when parliament opens, the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) will be the Speaker of the House of Commons." This was long before Margaret had told Pierre, or anything like that. I think that the hon. member will do a tremendous job for us here.

Sir, I already complimented you because I held your position once and I know the dangers of being deputy speaker. There are more dangers in being deputy speaker than there are in being Speaker, and perhaps, Mr. Deputy Speaker, you will allow me to tell the rest of the members what those dangers are. Consider the following: in 1957, the deputy speaker, a Mr. Robinson, was defeated in his attempt for re-election. The next deputy speaker was Mr. Courtemanche, and where is he today? The next one was Mr. Sevigny, followed by Jacques Flynn, now opposition leader in the Senate, followed by Mr. Paul Martineau and then Gordon C. Chown. All those gentleman were defeated.
Then comes the honourable exception to this litany of gloom, Mr. Lucien Lamoureux, who was deputy speaker from 1963 to 1965, and who defied the curse upon deputy speakers. But then behold Mr. Batten. The next one, the present Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) had sense enough to escape while escape was still good, and went into the ministry after a decent interval between deputy speaker and being a parliamentary secretary. Then came Mr. Honey, my immediate predecessor, now Judge Honey.
So now it behooves a person who walked down this death valley, like myself, and came through, to become a backbencher. But it was not easy, and a legitimate question was raised in the campaign: why vote for somebody who is not apt to be able to speak in the House of Commons? This has mixed blessings. He may get another position of greater worth, and so they would get some satisfaction that way.
I did not like to tell them what I thought was likely to happen, that I would be a backbencher after the election was over. I was caught between the devil and the deep blue sea.
The problem is that no great minds such as those of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) concentrated on the problem of the Deputy Speaker-that his hands are literally tied once he takes the chair.
In this House the practice has been to keep the Speaker in that position or, when he decides to go, to give him some recognition. But you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, are in a different category entirely. You suffer the handicap I did, that of not being able to participate in debate, and to a lesser extent your assistants suffer the same disability. The only way I can see to overcome this is to take some new step for the Deputy Speaker and his assistants, such as setting aside time in which they could make short speeches-I presume they would be of a non-partisan nature. In that way their constituents would feel that their concerns were being looked after in parliament. That is the only solution I can see for yourself and others, before you who take that march down Death Valley that I had to come through in my time.
There is another matter which is personal. On the defeat of the government on the vote last spring, at that moment the rights and privileges, pay and allowances of Deputy Speakers ceased. I am not making a plea for myself but for you, Sir. You have headed the Canadian delegation to Cuba and you are undoubtedly finding now that you have
November 21, 1974

to carry out a quasi-diploma tic function. You are receiving visitors from abroad.
I led a delegation to South Korea, and the business of that delegation did not end the night the government was defeated. I had to come back to Ottawa to complete the work. It was a labour of love, but it was not paid labour. I think the supposition that the Deputy Speaker's duties end when a session of parliament ends should be examined with a view to making redress. I do not ask it for myself, and I would refuse it if it were offered, but I ask it in light of your particular circumstances.
There is much more I could say, Mr. Speaker. I never did get around to talking about the ten minute speech as the cornerstone of parliamentary debate, but perhaps I will have an opportunity to do so later in the session.
